Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-to-agent-email.html (updated 2026-08-31)

Guide · Agent to agent

# When two agents email each other

Free and durable by default. Not because email is elegant — because it needs no shared infrastructure and a human can read the whole exchange when something breaks.

Two agents, two addresses, no broker to run and nothing to agree on in advance.

Free · Durable · Auditable

# researcher → writer

POST /v1/mail/send

to: writer@mailgi.xyz

subject: "Handoff: batch 41"

# =>

{ "messageId": "eaaaaab" }

# readable by the other side

# in a few seconds

## Why email, of all things

Three real reasons. Technical elegance is not among them.

### No shared infrastructure

A queue requires both agents to reach the same broker, which means one of you runs it and the other gets credentials. Two agents built by different people at different companies can email each other with no such agreement — the address is the entire integration surface.

### Durable and auditable for free

The whole exchange sits in two mailboxes. When a handoff goes wrong at 3am, the evidence is already there in a form a human can open and read, in order, without a log aggregator or a replay tool. You get this by default rather than by building it.

### A human can step in mid-conversation

Copy a person on a handoff and they are simply in the loop — they can read it, and they can reply into it from any mail client on any device. No queue offers that, because a queue has no interface a person already knows how to use.

## Both agents, in one script

Registration is unauthenticated, so bringing a second agent into existence costs one HTTP call and nothing else.

### Give each one an address

No quota on how many agents you create. A dedicated address per role is the normal pattern, not an extravagance.

Each key belongs with the process that uses it. Keys are shown once.

```
reg () {
  curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"label\":\"$1\"}"
}

A=$(reg researcher); B=$(reg writer)

A_KEY=$(echo "$A" | jq -r .apiKey)
A_ADDR=$(echo "$A" | jq -r .emailAddress)
B_KEY=$(echo "$B" | jq -r .apiKey)
B_ADDR=$(echo "$B" | jq -r .emailAddress)

sleep 3   # provisioning

# => blank-reindeer@mailgi.xyz
# => artificial-hamster@mailgi.xyz
```

### Hand work across

Put the machine-readable payload in the body and a human-readable summary in the subject. The same message then serves both an agent parsing JSON and a person scanning the mailbox to find out what happened.

A step or hop counter in the payload is what stops a loop later. Add it now; it costs one field.

```
# A → B, with a payload and a hop count
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail/send \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $A_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "$(jq -n --arg to "$B_ADDR" '{
        to:      [$to],
        subject: "Handoff: batch 41",
        textBody: ({
          step:   "draft",
          hop:    1,
          source: "rows 1-500",
          notes:  "figures verified, prose needed"
        } | tojson)
      }')"

# => {"messageId":"eaaaaab"}
```

### Receive, work, answer

B polls its own inbox, takes what is unseen from an address it recognises, and acts. Note from[0].email — the field is an array of objects, and comparing it to a string is the single most common mistake against this API.

Marking seen is what stops the next pass reprocessing the same message. There is no locking, so if two workers share a key, coordinate them yourself.

```
while true; do
  curl -s https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $B_KEY" \
  | jq -r --arg peer "$A_ADDR" '
      .messages[]
      | select(.seen == false)
      | select(.from[0].email == $peer)
      | .id' \
  | while read -r ID; do

      JOB=$(curl -s https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail/$ID \
              -H "Authorization: Bearer $B_KEY" \
            | jq -r '.bodyValues[.textBody[0].partId].value')

      HOP=$(echo "$JOB" | jq -r '.hop // 0')
      [ "$HOP" -ge 5 ] && { echo "hop limit" >&2; continue; }

      RESULT=$(do_the_work "$JOB")

      curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail/send \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $B_KEY" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "$(jq -n --arg to "$A_ADDR" --arg r "$RESULT" \
                    --argjson h "$((HOP + 1))" '{
              to:[$to],
              subject:"Re: Handoff: batch 41",
              textBody: ({step:"done", hop:$h, result:$r} | tojson)
            }')"

      curl -s -X PATCH https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail/$ID/flags \
        -H "Authorization: Bearer $B_KEY" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"seen":true}'
    done
  sleep 3
done
```

## Rules that keep it from going wrong

hop < 5

### Bound every exchange

Nothing in email stops two agents replying to each other forever. Carry a hop count and refuse past a maximum. Two agents that each politely acknowledge the other will run until you notice.

allowlist

### Only answer known senders

These addresses are publicly reachable — anyone can write to them. Match on the sender address and the subject you expect, and ignore anything else rather than handing it to a model.

untrusted

### Inbound mail is input, not instruction

A message from another agent is data from outside your trust boundary, even when the sender looks familiar — addresses are trivially forged. Never let its contents choose which tool to run.

seen

### Mark processed, immediately

The seen flag is your only idempotency mechanism. Set it as soon as a message is handled or a crash mid-loop means the work runs twice.

own allowance

### Internal mail has its own quota

Agent-to-agent mail on @mailgi.xyz costs nothing and is counted separately — 1,000 an hour and 5,000 a day per agent — so it never eats into the limits for mail to people.

poll or hook

### Latency is your poll interval

Delivery between agents takes seconds; the wait after that is your own interval. A webhook removes it — but if both agents are yours, a queue is the better tool anyway.

## When you should use a queue instead

If both agents are yours, run in the same system, and you already have Redis or SQS or Postgres in the stack — use that. It will be faster, it has real delivery semantics, and it has locking, which email does not. Email earns its place when the two sides are separately owned, or when a human needs to be able to read and join the conversation. Choosing it for two processes in the same container is choosing the slower, weaker option for no benefit.

The quota is still a design constraint, not a footnote: 5,000 internal sends a day per agent is about three and a half a minute, sustained. That is plenty for agents handing work to each other, and the wrong shape for a stream of events — which is what a queue is for.

The other honest limit: there is no delivery guarantee you can inspect. A queue tells you a message was acknowledged. Email tells you it was accepted for delivery, which is not the same thing — so build the acknowledgement into your own protocol, as a reply, rather than assuming a send that returned 200 was received.

## Questions, answered

Q: Why would AI agents email each other instead of using an API or a queue?

A: Three reasons, and none is that email is technically superior. It needs no shared infrastructure, so two agents built by different people at different companies can coordinate without either running a broker or agreeing on a protocol. It's durable and auditable by default, because the whole exchange sits in two mailboxes a human can open. And a person can join at any point just by being copied in. If both agents are yours and run in the same system, a real queue is the better tool.

Q: Is agent-to-agent email free on Mailgi?

A: Free, yes, and on its own allowance. Mail from one agent to another on @mailgi.xyz costs nothing and is counted separately from mail to the outside world: up to 1,000 an hour and 5,000 a day per sending agent, and it never draws on the external limits of 100 a day per API key and 300 a day per agent. It is capped rather than unlimited so that a cluster of agents cannot fan mail out at no cost; for high-volume handoffs a queue is still the better tool.

Q: How fast is agent-to-agent email delivery?

A: Typically readable within a few seconds, because it's delivered internally rather than crossing the public internet. The latency an agent actually experiences is then its own polling interval — every two or three seconds for tight handoffs, every minute for background work. A webhook removes that wait, though for two agents you control a queue is usually a better tool than either.

Q: How do you stop two AI agents emailing each other in a loop?

A: Nothing in the protocol prevents it, so it's on you. Put a hop counter or step name in the message and refuse to act past a maximum. Make each agent respond only to subjects it recognises rather than to anything that arrives. And never reply automatically to a message the agent can't classify — an unrecognised message answered with a generic reply is exactly how a loop starts.

Q: Can an AI agent tell who really sent a message?

A: Only weakly, and this matters. Mail from another Mailgi agent on the shared domain is delivered internally, so the sender address is reliable in practice. Mail from outside is only as trustworthy as its DKIM and SPF, which Mailgi checks but doesn't currently expose per-message in the API. Treat inbound content as untrusted input regardless of sender — never let it decide which tool an agent runs.

## Two agents, two curl commands

Registration takes no credentials and no signup. You can have both talking in under a minute.

Set one up →


---

Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/mcp.html (updated 2026-10-31)

MCP server

# Email for agents, as MCP tools

A hosted Model Context Protocol server at https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp. Point Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor at it and the agent can register an address, send, read and file mail — with nothing to install on the server side.

Every tool is the REST API, called for you. Same limits, same billing, same errors.

Streamable HTTP · Stateless · Headers for auth

# endpoint

https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp

# headers decide which tools work

Authorization: Bearer amb_… → agent tools

X-Mailgi-Session: <token> → org tools

(neither) → public tools only

## What it is

The MCP server runs inside the Mailgi API itself. Each tool forwards to an existing REST endpoint and returns that endpoint's response, so a tool call and the equivalent curl behave identically: the same validation, the same rate limits, the same metering against the same wallet. Nothing is cached or reshaped in between. The server is stateless — there is no MCP session to keep alive — and credentials travel as HTTP headers on the connection, not as tool arguments.

The server also exposes one resource, mailgi://skill, which serves SKILL.md — the plain-language guide to the API — so a client can load it as context without fetching the website.

## Connect a client

Transport is Streamable HTTP. Already have an API key? Add it as the Authorization header and you're done. Don't have one yet? Start without headers and follow the bootstrap below.

Claude Desktop's config file only launches local processes, so it reaches a remote server through the mcp-remote bridge, which needs Node.js. Cursor speaks HTTP directly.

Claude Code
Claude Desktop
Cursor

```
# With an agent API key
claude mcp add --transport http mailgi https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer amb_..."

# Org tools as well — add the dashboard session header
claude mcp add --transport http mailgi https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer amb_..." \
  --header "X-Mailgi-Session: <session token>"

# No credentials yet — public tools only, for bootstrap
claude mcp add --transport http mailgi https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp
```

```
// claude_desktop_config.json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mailgi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y", "mcp-remote", "https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp",
        "--header", "Authorization:${MAILGI_AUTH}"
      ],
      "env": { "MAILGI_AUTH": "Bearer amb_..." }
    }
  }
}
// The env indirection keeps the space in "Bearer amb_..."
// from being split when the arguments are passed on.
```

```
// .cursor/mcp.json (project) or ~/.cursor/mcp.json (global)
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mailgi": {
      "url": "https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer amb_..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Bootstrap: from nothing to a key

The server has no OAuth, so a credential can't be attached to the connection for you. The agent obtains one through a tool, and a human puts it into the client config once.

### An agent of its own

Connect with no headers and ask the agent to call register_agent (optionally with a label, or a domainToken and localPart to claim an address on a company domain). It returns the email address and an API key starting amb_ — shown exactly once. Re-add the server with Authorization: Bearer amb_… and the agent tools appear. In Claude Code that is claude mcp remove mailgi followed by the add command above.

### Org admin, by emailed code

For the organisation tools — domains, members, registration tokens, the org wallet — the agent calls org_login_request_code with a human's email address. Mailgi emails that person a six-digit code; they tell the agent, which passes it to org_login_verify and gets back a dashboard session token. Add it to the connection as X-Mailgi-Session. Call org_logout to end that session when you're done with it.

### Both at once

The two headers are independent. Send both and the connection has agent and org tools together — for example an admin agent that creates a registration token with regtoken_create and hands it to another agent to self-register on the company domain.

## All 67 tools

Tool names map one-to-one to REST endpoints, and each behaves exactly like the endpoint it names. For request and response fields, read the endpoint in the API docs or SKILL.md. Tools that delete, revoke or remove carry the MCP destructiveHint annotation, so a client that honours it asks before calling them.

### Agent tools · 25 · need Authorization: Bearer amb_…

Everything an agent does with its own mailbox and wallet.

Agent tools

| Tool | REST endpoint | What it does |

| agent_get | GET /v1/agents/me | This agent's profile and address |

| agent_usage | GET /v1/agents/me/usage | This agent's usage, by day |

| agent_delete | DELETE /v1/agents/me | Delete the agent — permanent, burns the address destructive |

| mail_list | GET /v1/mail | List messages |

| mail_get | GET /v1/mail/{id} | Read a message with its body |

| mail_send | POST /v1/mail/send | Send a message (metered exactly like REST) |

| mail_delete | DELETE /v1/mail/{id} | Move a message to Trash destructive |

| mail_move | PATCH /v1/mail/{id}/move | Move a message to another mailbox |

| mail_set_flags | PATCH /v1/mail/{id}/flags | Set seen / flagged |

| mailbox_list | GET /v1/mailboxes | List mailboxes (folders) |

| mailbox_create | POST /v1/mailboxes | Create a mailbox |

| mailbox_rename | PATCH /v1/mailboxes/{id} | Rename a mailbox |

| mailbox_delete | DELETE /v1/mailboxes/{id} | Delete a mailbox destructive |

| apikey_create | POST /v1/apikeys | Create an API key |

| apikey_revoke | DELETE /v1/apikeys/{keyId} | Revoke an API key destructive |

| billing_get | GET /v1/billing | Wallet balance, prices, how to top up |

| billing_topup | POST /v1/billing/topup | Create a card top-up link for a human to pay |

| billing_transactions | GET /v1/billing/transactions | Wallet ledger |

| webhook_list | GET /v1/webhook-endpoints | List webhook endpoints |

| webhook_create | POST /v1/webhook-endpoints | Register a webhook endpoint for inbound mail |

| webhook_delete | DELETE /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id} | Delete a webhook endpoint destructive |

| webhook_deliveries | GET /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id}/deliveries | Recent delivery attempts |

| webhook_resend | POST /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id}/deliveries/{deliveryId}/resend | Re-queue a delivery |

| webhook_enable | POST /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id}/enable | Re-enable an endpoint switched off by failures |

What a human does in the dashboard at app.mailgi.xyz, with that human's role in each organisation.

### Public tools · 7 · no credentials

Bootstrap, paying for any agent's wallet by address, and a health check.

Public tools

| Tool | REST endpoint | What it does |

| register_agent | POST /v1/agents/register | Register an agent; returns the API key once |

| org_login_request_code | POST /v1/auth/email/request-code | Email a 6-digit login code |

| org_login_verify | POST /v1/auth/email/verify-code | Verify the code; returns a session token |

| topup_lookup | GET /v1/topup/lookup | Who a top-up for an address would pay for |

| topup_start | POST /v1/topup | Start a card payment for any agent's wallet |

| topup_status | GET /v1/topup/sessions/{sessionId} | Status of a top-up payment |

| health | GET /health/ready | Readiness of the API and mail server |

Not exposed over MCP: DID authentication (not available in the API either), OAuth sign-in redirects, signup attribution, and the inbound webhooks from Mailgi's own providers.

## Limits, stated plainly

### One config edit after bootstrap

A key obtained through register_agent or a session from org_login_verify doesn't attach itself to the connection. A human has to add the header to the client config and reconnect. Until then only the public tools work.

### No OAuth, so no hosted connectors yet

claude.ai and ChatGPT add remote MCP servers as hosted custom connectors, which authenticate with OAuth rather than a header you type in. The server doesn't implement OAuth, so it can't be used from those today. Clients where you control the headers — Claude Code, Claude Desktop through mcp-remote, Cursor — work.

### Org tools give an agent admin reach

A session token carries the signed-in human's role. An agent holding an owner's or admin's session can detach domains, remove members, revoke tokens and delete inboxes. The destructiveHint annotation only helps if your client asks before acting on it — only add X-Mailgi-Session to a connection you would trust with the dashboard, and end it with org_logout.

### Same limits and prices as REST

MCP is not a separate tier. A mail_send is metered and rate-limited exactly like POST /v1/mail/send — see pricing — and errors come back as the endpoint's own error.

## Not using MCP?

The same API is plain HTTP, a CLI and a TypeScript SDK, and SKILL.md teaches any agent to use it directly.

REST, CLI and SDK →
read SKILL.md →

Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/faq.html (updated 2026-10-31)

FAQ

# Everything people ask before they start

24 questions about giving an AI agent its own email address, answered against the live API.

Mailgi gives an AI agent its own real email address in one API call, with no human in the loop. Receiving is free, mail between your own agents is free, and mail to the outside world costs $0.0005 per recipient from a prepaid balance. Every answer below matches the live API; where something isn't built yet, it says so.

## Getting an address

Q: How does an AI agent get its own email address?

A: One unauthenticated POST to https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register. The response carries a readable address like buzzing-falcon@mailgi.xyz, a second alias address that delivers to the same inbox, and an API key that is shown once. No signup form, no OAuth, no human approval. The full walkthrough is in how to give an AI agent an email address (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-address.html).

Q: Does a human need to sign up first?

A: No. An agent can register itself on the shared @mailgi.xyz domain with no account, card or credentials. A human is only needed for a custom domain: they attach it in the dashboard and hand the agent a registration token.

Q: Can the agent use our own domain, like support@ourcompany.com?

A: Yes. A human attaches the domain at app.mailgi.xyz (https://app.mailgi.xyz) and publishes the DNS records it generates: TXT and MX for inbound, then DKIM, a MAIL FROM subdomain for SPF, and a recommended DMARC record for outbound. Once verified, they create a registration token, and the agent registers with domainToken and a localPart such as support. Custom domains cost nothing extra.

Q: How many agents or inboxes can I create?

A: There is no inbox fee and no quota on registration. Each agent is one mailbox; for another address, register another agent. One agent per role or per task is a normal pattern.

Q: Can an agent delete its own address?

A: Yes, with DELETE /v1/agents/me. It is permanent and burns the address: a deleted local part can never be registered again, by anyone. To start clean, register a new agent instead.

## Receiving and reading

Q: Can an AI agent receive verification codes by email?

A: Yes. That is the most common reason to give an agent an address. Register, trigger the signup, poll GET /v1/mail every few seconds until the message arrives, then read the code from the body. See receiving a verification code (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-verification.html) for working code and the four mistakes that make it flaky.

Q: How does an agent find out that new mail has arrived?

A: Poll GET /v1/mail, or register an HTTPS webhook with POST /v1/webhook-endpoints. The webhook is a signed notification (HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and body) with the sender, time, size and a fetch URL, never the content. There is no WebSocket or long-poll.

Q: Can an agent search its inbox?

A: No. There is no full-text, subject, sender or date search. You can list by folder, page and sort, then match messages yourself. Unknown query parameters are ignored rather than rejected, so ?q=invoice returns the whole inbox.

Q: Does Mailgi support attachments?

A: Not yet. There is no attachments field on send; send a link instead.

Q: Can an agent reply in the same thread?

A: Not with threading headers. Send a new message with “Re: ” in the subject; most clients group it correctly by subject and participants, but there is no In-Reply-To header and no thread ID in the API.

Q: Can an agent organise mail into folders?

A: Yes. Create, rename and delete folders with /v1/mailboxes, move messages with PATCH /v1/mail/<id>/move and mark them read with PATCH /v1/mail/<id>/flags. Folders work well as ticket status in a support inbox.

## Sending and deliverability

Q: Will mail from an agent land in spam?

A: Every domain sends with DKIM, SPF and DMARC. On the shared @mailgi.xyz domain they are already in place; on your own domain Mailgi generates the records and refuses to send until they verify. Reputation on the shared domain is protected by conservative sending limits; on your own domain it is yours alone.

Q: What are the sending limits?

A: All apply at once and the lowest wins: 100 a day per API key; 50 an hour and 300 a day per agent; on a custom domain, 100 a day for the first three days, 1,000 a day up to thirty days, and 5,000 a day after that; on the shared @mailgi.xyz domain, one collective bucket of 500 an hour and 5,000 a day. Mail between Mailgi agents has its own allowance of 1,000 an hour and 5,000 a day per agent. Receiving and reading are not limited.

Q: Can I use Mailgi for newsletters or cold outreach?

A: No. Mailgi has no lists, imports or campaigns. Every send is one explicit API call naming its own recipients, at most 50 per field, and the limits above are deliberately too low for bulk mail.

Q: Can two agents email each other?

A: Yes, and it is free. Mail to any @mailgi.xyz address or to your organisation's own domains costs nothing and is counted separately from external sending. See agent-to-agent email (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-to-agent-email.html).

## Pricing and billing

Q: How much does Mailgi cost?

A: Receiving is free, and so is mail between your own agents. Mail that leaves Mailgi is pay-as-you-go from a prepaid balance: $0.0005 per external recipient, plus $0.02 once the first time an agent writes to an address that has never written to it. Storage above 10 MB per mailbox is $0.25 per GB-month. No subscription. Details on the pricing page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html).

Q: What is the $0.02 introduction charge?

A: A one-time charge the first time an agent writes to an address that has never written to it. Anyone whose DKIM-signed message reaches the agent becomes a known contact for free, so replying to customers, services and verification senders costs only the per-email price.

Q: What happens when the balance runs out?

A: A send the balance cannot cover is refused whole with 402 PAYMENT_REQUIRED, itemised, and nothing is charged. Receiving keeps working. The error carries a top-up link the agent can forward to whoever pays.

Q: How do I top up, and do I need an account?

A: Anyone can top up any agent by card at app.mailgi.xyz/topup (https://app.mailgi.xyz/topup), with no Mailgi account. The minimum is $5 plus any sales tax or VAT; Stripe is the merchant of record. An agent can also request a checkout link with POST /v1/billing/topup.

## Tools and integrations

Q: Is there an MCP server?

A: Yes, hosted at https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp (Streamable HTTP). It works with Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor, and every tool is a 1:1 proxy of a REST endpoint with the same limits and billing. It has no OAuth yet, so it cannot be added as a claude.ai or ChatGPT connector. Setup is on the MCP server page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/mcp.html).

Q: Is there an SDK or CLI?

A: Yes: npm install @mailgi/mailgi gives you the TypeScript SDK and the mailgi CLI. Neither is required; everything works over plain HTTP from any language.

Q: What is SKILL.md?

A: SKILL.md (https://www.mailgi.xyz/SKILL.md) is the whole API written in plain language for an agent to read at runtime. Point an agent at it and it can register, send and read mail without an SDK. It is versioned and tracks the live API. The docs page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/docs.html) explains how it differs from the OpenAPI spec and llms.txt.

## Security and privacy

Q: Where is mail stored?

A: Mailbox content is stored in Germany, and outbound mail relays through AWS in Ireland. The privacy page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/privacy.html) lists every sub-processor and where each one runs.

Q: How do I verify that a webhook came from Mailgi?

A: Compute HMAC-SHA256 over the x-mailgi-timestamp header, a dot, and the raw request body, using the secret returned when you created the endpoint, and compare it to x-mailgi-signature in constant time. Reject timestamps more than a few minutes old.

Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/docs.html (updated 2026-10-31)

Docs

# One API, four ways to read it

Mailgi is a REST API at api.mailgi.xyz. Here is which documentation to open, depending on whether you are a person, a tool or an agent.

Mailgi's API is documented four times, for four different readers. SKILL.md is for an agent, Swagger UI for a developer, openapi.json for tooling, and llms.txt for an AI crawler. They describe the same REST API at https://api.mailgi.xyz, and the MCP server and SDK wrap it one-to-one.

## Pick the surface for your reader

Same API, different shapes. If you are not sure, an agent wants SKILL.md and a person wants the guides.

| Surface | Who it's for | What it is | Use it when |

| SKILL.md (https://www.mailgi.xyz/SKILL.md) | An agent | The whole API in plain language, versioned, small enough for one context window. | You want an agent to onboard itself and act on the API directly. |

| Swagger UI (https://api.mailgi.xyz/docs) | A developer | Interactive explorer for every endpoint, with request and response schemas. | You want to try a call in the browser or check a field. |

| openapi.json (https://api.mailgi.xyz/openapi.json) | Tooling | The machine-readable OpenAPI spec. | You are generating a client or validating requests. |

| MCP server (https://www.mailgi.xyz/mcp.html) | An MCP client | https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp: every REST endpoint as a tool. | You use Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor. |

| @mailgi/mailgi (https://www.npmjs.com/package/@mailgi/mailgi) | A Node developer | TypeScript SDK and the mailgi CLI, methods 1:1 with REST. | You'd rather call typed methods than fetch. |

| llms.txt (https://www.mailgi.xyz/llms.txt) | An LLM crawler | A one-page site summary with links to everything above. | An assistant needs to find the right page quickly. |

## The whole loop in three calls

Every Mailgi integration starts here. Mail between Mailgi addresses is free, so this costs nothing to run.

### Register, send, read

Base URL https://api.mailgi.xyz. Authenticated calls take Authorization: Bearer amb_….

Wait a couple of seconds after registering before the first send: the mailbox is provisioned asynchronously. Retry once on a 5xx.

```
# 1. Register: no auth, no signup form
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"label":"my-agent"}'
# => {"emailAddress":"buzzing-falcon@mailgi.xyz","apiKey":"amb_..."}

# 2. Send (free between Mailgi addresses)
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail/send \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"to":["buzzing-falcon@mailgi.xyz"],"subject":"Hi","textBody":"Hello"}'

# 3. Read the inbox
curl -s https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"
```

## Endpoints at a glance

The full reference, with every field and error code, is in SKILL.md (https://www.mailgi.xyz/SKILL.md) and Swagger (https://api.mailgi.xyz/docs). Errors are always {"error":{"code","message"}}; match on the code, not the status.

| Endpoint | Auth | What it does |

| POST /v1/agents/register | none | Create an agent and its mailbox; returns the address and an API key (shown once). |

| GET /v1/mail | API key | List messages: folder, limit, position, sort. No search. |

| GET /v1/mail/<id> | API key | One message with its text and HTML body. |

| POST /v1/mail/send | API key | Send: to, cc, bcc, subject, textBody, htmlBody, replyTo. Other fields are ignored. |

| /v1/mailboxes | API key | List, create, rename and delete folders. |

| /v1/webhook-endpoints | API key | Signed notifications when mail arrives; deliveries log, resend, re-enable. |

| /v1/apikeys | API key | Create, list and revoke extra keys. |

| GET /v1/billing | API key | Balance, wallet standing, live prices, top-up links. |

| GET /health/ready | none | Readiness: database and mail server. |

## Guides that go further

### How to give an AI agent an email address (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-address.html)

The options, how each fails, and the setup in depth, including DKIM, SPF and DMARC.

### Receiving a verification code (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-verification.html)

Register, poll, extract the code, and avoid the four common failure modes.

### Running a support inbox (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-support-inbox.html)

Custom-domain setup, folders as ticket status, and replies without threading headers.

Limits, pricing, webhooks, MCP and storage, answered in one place.

Changelog

# What shipped, and when

Customer-facing changes to the API, SDK, dashboard and docs, newest first. Dates are when each change went live, taken from the commit history.

2026-10-31

## Hosted MCP server

- Mailgi is now an MCP server at https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp (Streamable HTTP, stateless). Every tool is a 1:1 proxy of a REST endpoint, with the same limits and billing. Works with Claude Code, Claude Desktop and Cursor. Setup (https://www.mailgi.xyz/mcp.html).

- SKILL.md 1.6.0 documents it in §15.

2026-10-30

## Pay-as-you-go pricing

- Receiving stays free, and so does mail between your own agents. Mail that leaves Mailgi is paid from a prepaid balance: $0.0005 per external recipient, $0.02 once per new address, and $0.25 per GB-month of storage above 10 MB. Pricing (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html).

- Anyone can top up any agent by card at app.mailgi.xyz/topup, without an account. A send the balance cannot cover is refused whole with an itemised 402 PAYMENT_REQUIRED.

- Reads carry a billing notice when the balance runs low, with a top-up link the agent can forward.

- TypeScript SDK and CLI 0.2.0 on npm: PaymentRequiredError, the billing notice, and webhook types.

2026-09-03

## Inbound webhooks

- Register an HTTPS endpoint with POST /v1/webhook-endpoints and Mailgi POSTs a signed notification when mail arrives: sender, time, size and a fetch URL, never the content. Delivery log, resend and re-enable included, in the API and the dashboard.

- Polling still works and is still the simpler choice for most agents.

2026-09-01

## Agent-to-agent mail gets its own allowance

- Mail between Mailgi agents is counted on its own allowance (1,000 an hour, 5,000 a day per agent), so coordinating with other agents never uses your external sending quota.

- Three working guides: verification codes (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-verification.html), support inboxes (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-support-inbox.html) and agent-to-agent email (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-to-agent-email.html).

2026-08-30

- SKILL.md is versioned and published as an OpenClaw skill on ClawHub (https://clawhub.ai/oyagev/skills/mailgi).

- New pages: how to give an AI agent an email address (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agent-email-address.html), the comparison (https://www.mailgi.xyz/vs-resend-postmark-mailgun.html) and pricing with every limit stated (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html).

2026-08-26

## Custom domains send with your own DKIM, SPF and DMARC

- Once a domain's inbound records verify, the dashboard generates the outbound set: DKIM under Mailgi's own selector, a MAIL FROM subdomain for SPF alignment, and a recommended DMARC record. Sending stays blocked until they verify.

- Dashboard sign-in by email and a one-time code.

2026-08-25

## Organisations and custom domains

- Attach your own domain, verify it over DNS, and issue registration tokens so agents register chosen addresses like support@yourdomain.com.

- Sending caps per agent and per organisation, scaled by domain age, with automatic suspension on bounces and complaints.

2026-04-18

## TypeScript SDK and CLI

- npm install @mailgi/mailgi: a typed client whose methods map 1:1 to the REST API, plus the mailgi command-line tool.

Comparison

# The best email API for AI agents, honestly ranked

Eight options compared on what decides an agent build: whether it gets a real mailbox, whether a human has to sign up first, and what it costs. Including where we lose.

Short answer, as of 31 October 2026: AgentMail is the most complete email API for AI agents if a human can sign up once. Mailgi is the one to use if the agent must create its own address and send with no human and no wallet. Resend now has threaded Inboxes and is the natural choice for teams already on Resend. If the agent only sends, use a transactional provider.

## The shortlist, side by side

Ordered by how much of the agent problem each solves out of the box, not by who wrote the page. Yes, we wrote it; we put AgentMail first on capability.

Last verified: 2026-10-31 against each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages. Pricing moves; re-check before you commit.

| Product | Kind | Receiving | Human needed to start? | Free | Paid from |

| AgentMail | Agent-native | Mailbox, threads, full-text search, IMAP/SMTP, WebSockets | Optional; can't send until one is attached (or pay from a USDC wallet) | 3 inboxes, 3k/mo, 100/day | $20/mo |

| Mailgi | Agent-native | Mailbox, folders, webhooks; no search or threading | No human, sends immediately | Receiving free; pay per send | Prepaid from $5 |

| Resend | Developer email + Inboxes | Inboxes (Oct 2026): threads, labels, search; inbound webhooks | Human signup and verified domain | 3k/mo, 100/day; 3 inboxes | $20/mo |

| Nylas Agent Accounts | Agent mailboxes + calendar | Mailbox, threads, IMAP/SMTP (paid) | Human signup for the API key | 3 accounts, 3k emails | $15/mo |

| mails.ai | Agent sending + replies | Reply events and webhooks | Human signup | 1 agent, 3k/mo | $20/mo |

| Cloudflare Email Service | Primitives on Workers | Routing to your Worker; storage is yours | Cloudflare account | Receiving free | $5/mo Workers |

| Postmark | Transactional | Parse webhook (Pro and up) | Human signup | 100/mo | $15/mo; inbound $16.50 |

| Mailgun / SendGrid | Transactional | Routes or Inbound Parse webhook | Human signup | Mailgun 100/day; SendGrid 60-day trial | $15 / $19.95 |

## How to pick

Four questions settle it faster than any ranking. They are explained in depth in how to choose an email API for an AI agent (https://www.mailgi.xyz/choosing-an-email-api-for-ai-agents.html).

### Does the agent need to read mail, or only send it?

Send-only: use Postmark, Resend or SES and stop reading. Needs to read: you want a mailbox, so AgentMail, Mailgi, Resend Inboxes or Nylas.

### Can a human sign up once?

If yes, AgentMail, Resend Inboxes and Nylas are all more feature-complete than Mailgi. If the agent must create its own address with nobody awake, Mailgi is built for exactly that.

### Do you need search, threads or attachments today?

Mailgi has none of them yet. AgentMail and Resend Inboxes have search and threads; the transactional providers handle attachments.

### How does the bill scale?

Plans with included volume (AgentMail, Resend, Nylas) are cheaper per message at steady high volume. Mailgi has no monthly fee and free receiving, so it is cheapest for many low-traffic agents; its $0.02 first-contact charge makes it expensive for cold outreach to many new addresses, which it is not for.

## Each one in a paragraph

### 1. AgentMail: the most complete

YC-backed, $6M seed, threads, full-text search, IMAP and SMTP, WebSockets, pods for multi-tenant products, SOC 2 on the $200 plan. The default answer if a human can sign up once. See AgentMail alternative (https://www.mailgi.xyz/agentmail-alternative.html) for where we differ.

### 2. Mailgi: no human, anywhere

One unauthenticated POST gives a program a real address that can send immediately. Free receiving, free mail between your agents, free custom domains, pay-as-you-go sending. No search, threading headers or attachments yet.

### 3. Resend: best developer experience, now with inboxes

Inbound since November 2025 and threaded Inboxes since 22 October 2026. A strong pick if your humans already use Resend. See Resend for AI agents (https://www.mailgi.xyz/resend-for-ai-agents.html).

### 4. Nylas Agent Accounts: mailbox plus calendar

Hosted mailboxes and calendars for agents, US or EU region on every plan. Beta since April 2026.

### 5. mails.ai: built around replies

Sending plus reply events with intent classification and a prompt-injection scanner. New in 2026.

### 6. Cloudflare Email Service: cheapest primitives

If your agent already runs on Workers, receiving is free and sending is $0.35 per thousand after 3,000 included. You build the mailbox yourself.

### 7. Postmark, Mailgun, SendGrid: transactional

Excellent at sending. Receiving is a webhook you catch and store. Right for notifications, wrong for an agent that needs to look back at last week's mail.

### Not on the list: the Gmail API

Fine for one internal agent; painful for anything shipped to users. See should your AI agent use Gmail? (https://www.mailgi.xyz/gmail-api-for-ai-agents.html)

## Questions, answered

Q: What is the best email API for AI agents?

A: If a human can sign up once and you need threads and search, AgentMail is the most complete option as of October 2026. If the agent must create its own address with no human involved, Mailgi is built for that. If the agent only sends, a transactional provider such as Postmark or Resend is the better choice.

Q: Which email APIs give each AI agent its own inbox?

A: AgentMail, Mailgi, Resend Inboxes and Nylas Agent Accounts all provide real mailboxes an agent can list and read. Postmark, Mailgun and SendGrid deliver inbound mail to a webhook instead, so you store it yourself.

Q: Is there a free email API for AI agents?

A: Several have free tiers: AgentMail (3 inboxes, 3,000 emails a month), Resend (3,000 a month), Nylas (3 accounts), mails.ai (1 agent). Mailgi has no monthly fee: receiving, registration and mail between your own agents are free, and outbound mail is $0.0005 per recipient from a prepaid balance.

Q: Which email API has an MCP server?

A: AgentMail, Resend, mails.ai, Cloudflare and Mailgi all offer one. Mailgi's is hosted at https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp and every tool maps one-to-one to a REST endpoint.

# An AgentMail alternative, and when not to switch

AgentMail is the most complete email API for agents. Mailgi differs on one thing that matters to some builds: a program can register and send with no human at all.

Mailgi and AgentMail both give AI agents real mailboxes over an API. AgentMail is more mature, with threads, full-text search, IMAP, WebSockets and SOC 2. Mailgi lets an agent register itself and send immediately with no human and no wallet, has no per-inbox fee, and receives for free. Choose on that, not on a feature count.

## Mailgi vs AgentMail, line by line

Facts from AgentMail's own pricing page and API docs.

Last verified: 2026-10-31 against each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages. Pricing moves; re-check before you commit.

| | Mailgi | AgentMail |

| Agent registers itself | Yes: one POST, can send immediately | Yes, but can't send until a human is attached; or pay per call from a USDC wallet ($2 per inbox) |

| Inbox pricing | No per-inbox fee | 3 free; 10 on $20/mo; 150 on $200/mo |

| Receiving | Free, not counted | Counts toward plan limits |

| Sending | $0.0005 per recipient, $0.02 once per new address | Included in plan: 3k/mo free, 10k/mo on $20 |

| Custom domains | Free on every agent | Paid plans (10 on $20/mo) |

| Threading | No (Re: subject only) | Yes |

| Search | No | Full-text |

| IMAP / SMTP / WebSocket | No / No / No | Yes / Yes / Yes |

| Webhooks | Yes, signed, no content | Yes |

| MCP server | Yes, hosted | Yes, hosted |

| Attachments | No | Yes |

| SOC 2 | No | Type II on $200/mo |

| Data location | Mail stored in Germany | US; EU on Enterprise |

## Pick AgentMail if

### You need threads, search or attachments now

We don't have them. AgentMail does, plus IMAP and WebSockets.

### A human can sign up once

Then our main difference doesn't apply to you, and AgentMail is the more mature product.

### You need a SOC 2 report

AgentMail has a Type II report on its $200 plan. We don't have one.

### You send high, steady volume to new people

At 10,000 first-contact emails a month AgentMail's $20 plan is far cheaper than our $0.02 introduction charge. Mailgi is not built for outreach.

## Pick Mailgi if

### The agent has to create its own address, unattended

One POST, no human, no wallet, and it can send straight away. That is the reason Mailgi exists.

### You run many agents with little traffic each

No per-inbox fee and free receiving: a thousand mostly idle agents cost nothing until they send.

### Most mail goes to people who wrote first

Anyone whose DKIM-signed mail reached the agent is a known contact; replying costs $0.0005.

### You want your own domain on day one, free

Custom domains are free and every agent on them shares the organisation's balance.

## Questions, answered

Q: What is the best AgentMail alternative?

A: It depends on why you're leaving. For agents that register themselves with no human, Mailgi. For a team already on Resend, Resend Inboxes. For mailbox plus calendar, Nylas Agent Accounts. If you need threads, search and SOC 2, AgentMail itself is still the strongest option.

Q: Can an AgentMail agent sign itself up without a human?

A: Partly. AgentMail's sign-up endpoint now makes the human email optional, but without one the inbox can only receive until a human is attached. An agent with a USDC wallet can instead pay per request over x402, $2 per inbox; AgentMail's docs don't say what such an inbox may send to.

Q: Is Mailgi cheaper than AgentMail?

A: For many agents with light traffic, yes: no monthly fee, no per-inbox fee and free receiving. For steady volume to new recipients, no: AgentMail's $20 plan includes 10,000 emails, while Mailgi charges $0.02 the first time an agent writes to each new address.

Q: Can I move from AgentMail to Mailgi?

A: Yes, but it is a rewrite of the mail calls, not a config change: Mailgi has its own REST API, SDK and MCP server, and no threading or search. Register a Mailgi agent per AgentMail inbox and point your domain's MX records at Mailgi when you are ready.

## Sources

- AgentMail pricing (https://www.agentmail.to/pricing)

- AgentMail agent sign-up API (https://agentmail.to/docs/api-reference/agent/sign-up.md)

- AgentMail agent sign-up limits (https://agentmail.to/docs/knowledge-base/agent-sign-up-limits.md)

- AgentMail x402 payments (https://agentmail.to/docs/integrations/x402.md)

- Mailgi pricing (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html)

# Resend for AI agents, now that it has inboxes

Resend launched Inboxes on 22 October 2026. Here is what that changes, and what still separates it from an API built for agents to sign up on their own.

Resend is no longer send-only: since 22 October 2026 its Inboxes give agents threaded mailboxes with search on your verified domain. Choose Resend if a human sets it up and you want threads, search and attachments. Choose Mailgi if agents must create their own addresses, receive more than they send, or keep mail longer than 30 days.

## Mailgi vs Resend for agents

Resend is a superb sending platform that now also has mailboxes. The questions below are the ones that matter for an agent.

Last verified: 2026-10-31 against each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages. Pricing moves; re-check before you commit.

| | Mailgi | Resend |

| Who creates the account | The agent, with one POST | A human, then verifies a domain |

| Mailbox for each agent | Yes, on @mailgi.xyz or your domain | Inboxes on your verified domain (since 22 Oct 2026) |

| Inbox pricing | No per-inbox fee | 3 included, then $1 each on paid plans |

| Receiving | Free, not counted | Counts toward your sending quota |

| Retention | Kept until deleted; $0.25/GB-month above 10 MB | 30 days on standard plans |

| Threads / search | No / No | Yes / Yes (Inboxes) |

| Attachments | No | Yes |

| Sending price | $0.0005 per recipient, no plan | Free 3k/mo; Pro $20/mo for 50k |

| MCP server | Yes | Yes |

## When Resend is the right call

### Your app already sends through Resend

Adding Inboxes keeps one vendor, one domain setup and one bill.

### Agents need threads, search or attachments

Resend Inboxes have all three; Mailgi has none yet.

### You send at volume

Pro's 50,000 emails for $20 beats per-message pricing for steady volume.

## When Mailgi fits better

### The agent must get its own address unattended

No human signup, no domain verification to start: one POST on the shared domain.

### Agents receive more than they send

Receiving is free on Mailgi and doesn't count against anything; on Resend it uses sending quota.

### Mail must outlive 30 days

A Mailgi mailbox keeps mail until the agent deletes it.

## Questions, answered

Q: Can Resend receive email for an AI agent?

A: Yes. Resend has had inbound since November 2025 and launched Inboxes, threaded mailboxes with folders, labels and search, on 22 October 2026. Inboxes need a verified domain, and received mail counts toward your sending quota.

Q: Can an AI agent create its own Resend account?

A: No. A human creates the Resend account and verifies a domain before any API key exists. Mailgi lets an agent register itself with one unauthenticated POST.

Q: Is Resend or Mailgi cheaper for an AI agent?

A: Resend is cheaper for steady sending volume (Pro is $20 for 50,000 emails). Mailgi is cheaper for agents that mostly receive or send little: no plan fee, free receiving, $0.0005 per external recipient and $0.02 once per new address.

# Should your AI agent use Gmail?

The Gmail API works for one internal agent. Shipping an agent that reads users' Gmail means OAuth verification, a yearly security assessment and access to everything in the mailbox.

Use the Gmail API only for an internal agent on your own Workspace account. For anything shipped to other people, restricted Gmail scopes require OAuth verification and a CASA security assessment renewed every 12 months, unverified apps are capped at 100 users, and the agent can read the user's entire mailbox. Giving the agent its own address, and forwarding it what it needs, avoids all of it.

## What it takes to ship an agent on Gmail

Fine for one internal agent on a Workspace account. Each step below applies once the agent serves users outside your organisation.

### A Cloud project and an OAuth consent screen

Before the agent reads one message: project, consent screen, scopes, and an OAuth flow each user clicks through.

### A 100-user cap until verified

Unverified apps can sign in at most 100 new users and show a warning screen.

### Restricted scopes mean a security assessment

Reading Gmail uses restricted scopes. Apps that handle that data on their own servers need a CASA assessment by an approved assessor, renewed every 12 months; Google says verification alone can take several weeks.

### The agent can read everything

The structural problem: an agent with access to a person's mailbox reads all of it, and everything it sends is from that person.

## Gmail API vs an agent's own address

Facts from Google's OAuth verification documentation.

Last verified: 2026-10-31 against each vendor's own pricing and documentation pages. Pricing moves; re-check before you commit.

| | Gmail API on a user's account | Mailgi address for the agent |

| Setup before the first read | Cloud project, consent screen, OAuth | One POST |

| Human involvement | Each user consents | None |

| Shipping to outside users | Verification and annual CASA assessment | Nothing extra |

| What the agent can read | The whole mailbox | Only mail sent to the agent |

| Sender identity | The human | The agent's own address or your domain |

| Cost | Free API; assessment costs | Receiving free; $0.0005 per external recipient |

## A pattern that keeps both

### Forward, don't grant

Give the agent its own address and have the human forward or CC it what it needs. The agent works from its inbox; the human's mailbox stays private.

### Reply from the agent's address

Customers see a stable address you control, with DKIM, SPF and DMARC on your own domain.

## Questions, answered

Q: Should my AI agent use the Gmail API?

A: For one internal agent on your own Workspace account, it is free and workable. For an agent used by people outside your organisation, the OAuth verification, 100-user cap before verification and annual CASA assessment for restricted scopes make it slow and costly, and the agent can read the whole mailbox. Giving the agent its own address avoids all of that.

Q: Can I create Gmail accounts for my AI agents?

A: Not programmatically for consumer Gmail, and accounts operated by bots risk being flagged. Workspace accounts are paid per user. An email API for agents gives each agent an address with one call.

Q: Does the Gmail API need a security assessment?

A: Apps using restricted Gmail scopes that access data through their own servers must pass a third-party CASA security assessment, renewed at least every 12 months. Internal Workspace apps and personal use are exempt.

## Sources

- Google: restricted scope verification (https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification)

- Google: unverified apps (https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/7454865)

- Mailgi pricing (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html)

# Email for an OpenAI Agents SDK agent

Give the agent its own inbox in one call, then hand it three function tools: send, list, read. About 40 lines of Python in total.

To give an OpenAI Agents SDK agent email, register an address with one POST to Mailgi, then expose three plain Python functions as function_tool: send_email, list_inbox and read_email. The agent can then receive verification codes, answer mail and write to people from its own address, with no OAuth and no shared human inbox.

## Give the agent an address

One call, no signup form. Do this once per agent and keep the key in your secrets store.

### Register

The response carries the address and an API key that is shown exactly once.

Wait a couple of seconds before the first send while the mailbox is provisioned.

```
# Once, outside the agent: give it an address and keep the key
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"label":"my-agent"}'
# => {"emailAddress":"buzzing-falcon@mailgi.xyz","apiKey":"amb_..."}

export MAILGI_API_KEY=amb_...   # shown once: store it
```

## Three tools, plain HTTP

Framework-free functions over the REST API, saved as mailgi_tools.py. Each was run against the live API before publishing.

### The three tools

Docstrings become the tool descriptions the model sees, so keep them short and literal.

from is a list of objects; the address is m['from'][0]['email']. Treating it as a string is the most common mistake with this API.

A 402 comes back as text with a top-up link rather than an exception, so the model can explain it.

```
import os, time, requests

API = "https://api.mailgi.xyz"
KEY = os.environ["MAILGI_API_KEY"]
H = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}


def send_email(to: str, subject: str, body: str) -> str:
    """Send a plain-text email from the agent's own address."""
    r = requests.post(f"{API}/v1/mail/send", headers=H,
                      json={"to": [to], "subject": subject, "textBody": body})
    if r.status_code == 402:
        return "Not sent: balance too low. Top up: " + r.json()["error"]["details"]["topupPage"]
    r.raise_for_status()
    return f"Sent, message id {r.json()['messageId']}"


def list_inbox(limit: int = 10) -> str:
    """List the newest messages: id, sender, subject, preview."""
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/v1/mail", headers=H, params={"limit": limit})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return "\n".join(
        f"{m['id']} | {m['from'][0]['email']} | {m['subject']} | {m['preview'][:80]}"
        for m in r.json()["messages"]) or "Inbox is empty."


def read_email(message_id: str) -> str:
    """Read one message's full text."""
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/v1/mail/{message_id}", headers=H)
    r.raise_for_status()
    m = r.json()
    body = m.get("textBody") or m.get("htmlBody") or ""
    if isinstance(body, list):  # JMAP parts
        body = "".join(m["bodyValues"][p["partId"]]["value"] for p in body)
    return f"From: {m['from'][0]['email']}\nSubject: {m['subject']}\n\n{body}"
```

## Wire them into OpenAI Agents SDK

### The agent

function_tool reads the type hints and docstring to build each tool's schema; the three functions need no SDK-specific code.

Tested with openai-agents 0.24. Uses whichever model your Agents SDK is configured for.

```
# pip install openai-agents requests
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool
import mailgi_tools as mail

agent = Agent(
    name="Mail agent",
    instructions=(
        "You have your own email address. Use list_inbox and read_email "
        "to check mail, and send_email to reply. Never invent a message id."
    ),
    tools=[function_tool(mail.send_email),
           function_tool(mail.list_inbox),
           function_tool(mail.read_email)],
)

result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "Check my inbox and summarise anything new.")
print(result.final_output)
```

## What the tools can't do yet

Better to know before the model tries.

### No search, no threads

There is no search parameter; list_inbox pages newest first and the model matches messages itself. Replies are new messages with “Re:” in the subject.

### No attachments

Send links instead. Incoming attachments are not exposed.

### Mail to strangers is metered

Sending to other @mailgi.xyz agents is free; to outside addresses it costs $0.0005 per recipient plus $0.02 the first time you write to a new address. With no balance, send_email returns the top-up link instead of raising, so the model can tell the user.

## Questions, answered

Q: How do I give an OpenAI agent an email address?

A: Register one with a single POST to https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register, store the API key it returns, and give the agent tools that call the Mailgi REST API to send, list and read mail. No OAuth or human signup is needed.

Q: Can an OpenAI Agents SDK agent receive verification codes?

A: Yes. Once it has its own address it can use list_inbox and read_email to find the code. Poll every few seconds after triggering the signup; most codes arrive within seconds.

Q: Is there an MCP server instead of function tools?

A: Yes, at https://api.mailgi.xyz/mcp. Function tools are simpler when you only need send, list and read; the MCP server exposes the whole API.

Q: What does it cost?

A: Registering and receiving are free, and so is mail between Mailgi agents. Mail to outside addresses costs $0.0005 per recipient plus $0.02 the first time an agent writes to a new address, from a prepaid balance.

# A LangChain agent with its own inbox

LangChain's create_agent plus three tools over the Mailgi API. The agent gets a real address, not a seat in your Gmail.

To build a LangChain email agent, register a Mailgi address with one POST, wrap three plain functions (send_email, list_inbox, read_email) with LangChain's tool decorator, and pass them to create_agent. The agent then reads and answers mail at its own address with no OAuth flow or shared inbox.

## Give the agent an address

One call, no signup form. Do this once per agent and keep the key in your secrets store.

### Register

The response carries the address and an API key that is shown exactly once.

Wait a couple of seconds before the first send while the mailbox is provisioned.

```
# Once, outside the agent: give it an address and keep the key
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"label":"my-agent"}'
# => {"emailAddress":"buzzing-falcon@mailgi.xyz","apiKey":"amb_..."}

export MAILGI_API_KEY=amb_...   # shown once: store it
```

### The three tools

Docstrings become the tool descriptions the model sees, so keep them short and literal.

from is a list of objects; the address is m['from'][0]['email']. Treating it as a string is the most common mistake with this API.

A 402 comes back as text with a top-up link rather than an exception, so the model can explain it.

```
import os, time, requests

API = "https://api.mailgi.xyz"
KEY = os.environ["MAILGI_API_KEY"]
H = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {KEY}"}


def send_email(to: str, subject: str, body: str) -> str:

    r = requests.post(f"{API}/v1/mail/send", headers=H,
                      json={"to": [to], "subject": subject, "textBody": body})
    if r.status_code == 402:
        return "Not sent: balance too low. Top up: " + r.json()["error"]["details"]["topupPage"]
    r.raise_for_status()
    return f"Sent, message id {r.json()['messageId']}"


def list_inbox(limit: int = 10) -> str:
    """List the newest messages: id, sender, subject, preview."""
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/v1/mail", headers=H, params={"limit": limit})
    r.raise_for_status()

        f"{m['id']} | {m['from'][0]['email']} | {m['subject']} | {m['preview'][:80]}"
        for m in r.json()["messages"]) or "Inbox is empty."


def read_email(message_id: str) -> str:
    """Read one message's full text."""
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/v1/mail/{message_id}", headers=H)
    r.raise_for_status()
    m = r.json()
    body = m.get("textBody") or m.get("htmlBody") or ""
    if isinstance(body, list):  # JMAP parts
        body = "".join(m["bodyValues"][p["partId"]]["value"] for p in body)
    return f"From: {m['from'][0]['email']}\nSubject: {m['subject']}\n\n{body}"
```

## Wire them into LangChain

### The agent

tool() turns each function into a LangChain tool, using its docstring as the description.

Tested with langchain 1.4. Swap the model string for any provider LangChain supports.

```
# pip install langchain langchain-anthropic requests
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.tools import tool
import mailgi_tools as mail

agent = create_agent(
    "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5",   # any chat model LangChain supports
    tools=[tool(mail.send_email), tool(mail.list_inbox), tool(mail.read_email)],
    system_prompt=(
        "You have your own email address. Use list_inbox and read_email "
        "to check mail, and send_email to reply. Never invent a message id."
    ),
)

result = agent.invoke(
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Any new mail? Summarise it."}]}
)
print(result["messages"][-1].content)
```

## What the tools can't do yet

Better to know before the model tries.

### No search, no threads

There is no search parameter; list_inbox pages newest first and the model matches messages itself. Replies are new messages with “Re:” in the subject.

### No attachments

Send links instead. Incoming attachments are not exposed.

### Mail to strangers is metered

Sending to other @mailgi.xyz agents is free; to outside addresses it costs $0.0005 per recipient plus $0.02 the first time you write to a new address. With no balance, send_email returns the top-up link instead of raising, so the model can tell the user.

## Questions, answered

Q: How do I give a LangChain agent email access?

A: Give it its own address rather than access to yours: register one with a single POST to Mailgi, then wrap send, list and read calls to the Mailgi REST API as LangChain tools and pass them to create_agent.

Q: Why not use the Gmail toolkit?

A: It works for your own inbox, but it needs OAuth, and the agent can read everything in that mailbox. For an agent shipped to other people, Gmail's restricted scopes also require verification and an annual security assessment.

Q: Can the agent reply in the same thread?

A: Not with threading headers. send_email starts a new message; put “Re:” and the original subject in the subject line and most mail clients group it correctly.

Q: Does it work with LangGraph?

A: Yes. create_agent returns a LangGraph graph, and the same tools work in any custom LangGraph node.

Guide

# Give your AI assistant its own email

Your assistant doesn't need your password. It needs an address of its own, and the mail you choose to send it.

Give your AI assistant its own email address instead of your password. Register one in a single API call, forward or CC it the mail it needs, and let it reply from its own address. You decide what it sees; it never has access to the rest of your mailbox, and you can revoke it without touching your own account.

## Why not just connect your Gmail?

### It reads everything

Mailbox access is all or nothing: bank mail, medical results, your partner's messages. An assistant with your inbox can be prompted by any email that lands in it.

### It speaks as you

Every message it sends comes from you. A mistake is your mistake, in your name.

### It is hard to take back

Revoking means OAuth settings, app passwords or a password change, and it may be locked into other things.

## Set it up in three steps

Free to set up: registration and receiving cost nothing.

### Register, forward, read

Use your mail client's filters to forward only what the assistant should handle, such as receipts, travel confirmations or a newsletter digest.

When you want it in a conversation, CC its address. It reads with its API key and replies from its own address.

With Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor, connect the MCP server (https://www.mailgi.xyz/mcp.html) instead of writing code.

```
# 1. Give the assistant its own address (once)
curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"label":"my-assistant"}'
# => {"emailAddress":"quiet-otter@mailgi.xyz","apiKey":"amb_..."}

# 2. In Gmail or Outlook, add a filter that forwards
#    receipts / travel / newsletters to quiet-otter@mailgi.xyz
#    (or just CC it when you want it involved)

# 3. The assistant reads its own inbox
curl -s "https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/mail?limit=20" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MAILGI_API_KEY"
```

## What it can do from its own inbox

### Sign up for things on your behalf

Its own address receives the verification code, so the account is the assistant's, not yours.

### Keep receipts and confirmations

File them into folders and answer “when does my flight leave?” from mail it already has.

### Write to people as itself

Replies come from its address. Mail to people who wrote first costs $0.0005; a first message to a new address adds $0.02 once.

### What it can't do yet

Search, threading headers and attachments aren't supported. It lists and reads messages and matches them itself.

## Questions, answered

Q: Should I give my AI assistant access to my Gmail?

A: Only if you are comfortable with it reading everything and sending as you. A safer pattern is to give the assistant its own address and forward or CC it what it needs.

Q: How do I give an AI assistant its own email address?

A: Register one with a single POST to https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register. It returns an address like quiet-otter@mailgi.xyz and an API key. No signup form or OAuth.

Q: Can I use my own domain for the assistant?

A: Yes. Attach the domain in the Mailgi dashboard, publish the DNS records it generates, then register the assistant as, say, assistant@yourdomain.com. Custom domains are free.

Q: Can I take the address away?

A: Yes. Revoke its API keys, or delete the agent. Your own mailbox is never involved.


---

Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/inbox-per-agent-vs-catch-all.html (updated 2026-10-31)

Decision guide

# Inbox per agent, or one catch-all?

Two ways to give many agents email. One of them turns your routing code into security code.

Give each agent its own inbox when agents have separate identities, credentials or customers; use a catch-all with routing only when one consumer reads everything anyway, such as a test harness. Inbox per agent costs a little more setup per agent and removes a whole class of misrouting and access bugs.

## The two designs, compared

A catch-all accepts mail for any address on a domain into one mailbox; your code reads the To header and dispatches. Inbox per agent gives each agent a real mailbox and key.

| | Inbox per agent | Catch-all + router |

| Setup | One registration per agent | One mailbox, routing code you maintain |

| Isolation | Each agent sees only its own mail | Router sees everything; a bug misroutes mail |

| Credentials | One key per agent, revocable alone | One shared credential |

| Sending identity | Each agent replies from its address | Need a send-as per address |

| Audit | Per-agent mailbox is the log | Rebuild per-agent history from routing logs |

| Cost shape | Per-inbox fees on some providers; none on Mailgi | One mailbox |

| Good for | Agents with distinct identities | Ephemeral addresses for tests, one consumer |

## Where catch-all goes wrong

### Routing is now security code

The To header decides which agent reads a message. BCC, forwarding and display-name tricks all land in the same box, and a routing bug hands one customer's mail to another customer's agent.

### Prompt injection reaches every agent

Any message to any address on the domain is read by the router first. With separate inboxes, a hostile message only ever reaches the one agent it was addressed to.

### Revoking one agent revokes all

One credential reads the shared mailbox. Taking one agent offline means rotating it for everyone.

## When catch-all is fine

### Test suites

Generating a fresh address per test run and reading them all from one place is exactly what a catch-all is good at.

### One agent, many aliases

If one agent legitimately handles every address, routing is just labelling.

## Inbox per agent on Mailgi

There is no catch-all on Mailgi; each address is an agent. Registration is free and has no quota, so one agent per role is the normal pattern.

### One call per agent

On your own domain, a human creates a registration token once in the dashboard, and each agent claims its own local part with domainToken and localPart.

Agents on an organisation's domain share the organisation's balance; mail between them is free.

```
# One token, several agents on your domain
for role in support sales billing; do
  curl -s -X POST https://api.mailgi.xyz/v1/agents/register \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"domainToken\":\"$TOKEN\",\"localPart\":\"$role\"}"
done
# => support@yourco.com, sales@yourco.com, billing@yourco.com
#    each with its own mailbox and API key
```

## Questions, answered

Q: Should each AI agent have its own email inbox?

A: Yes, when agents act for different customers, roles or tasks. Separate inboxes isolate mail, credentials and prompt-injection exposure, and each agent replies from its own address. A catch-all with a router is only simpler when one consumer reads everything anyway.

Q: What is a catch-all email address?

A: A domain setting that accepts mail sent to any address on the domain, including ones that were never created, and delivers it to one mailbox.

Q: Does Mailgi support catch-all addresses?

A: No. Each Mailgi address belongs to one agent with its own mailbox. Registering more agents is free and has no quota.

About

# Every agent deserves its own address

Agents shouldn't have to borrow ours. Why Mailgi exists, and what we hold ourselves to.

Mailgi is email infrastructure for AI agents. A program registers itself with one API call and gets a real, deliverable mailbox: it can receive verification codes, answer mail and write to people from its own address, on a shared domain or yours. Mailgi has been running since April 2026 and is small and early; this page says what that means.

## What we believe

### An agent should have its own address

Not a seat in a human's inbox, and not a send-only relay. Email is the one identity every service already accepts; an agent that has its own can sign up, be written to and be held accountable.

### No human in the loop to start

If a person has to click through a signup or read a code before an agent gets an address, the agent isn't really autonomous. Registration is one unauthenticated POST, and the abuse controls sit on sending instead.

### Receiving should be free

An agent that mostly listens shouldn't pay to listen. Receiving, mail between your own agents and custom domains cost nothing; mail to the outside world is paid per message.

### Say what isn't built

Search, threading headers and attachments aren't supported yet, and every page that matters says so. We'd rather lose a comparison than have an agent act on a feature we don't have.

## Where we are

### Early

No customer logos, testimonials or uptime figures on this site, because we don't have ones worth quoting yet. The footer's status light reads the live health check.

### Shipping in the open

The changelog (https://www.mailgi.xyz/changelog.html) lists every customer-facing release with its date. The website, SDKs and OpenAPI spec are public on GitHub (https://github.com/Mailgi).

### Built on boring parts

Stalwart mail server in Germany, Postgres in Frankfurt, outbound through AWS SES in Ireland, an API on Railway. The privacy page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/privacy.html) lists every processor and where it runs.

## Talk to a person

### hello@mailgi.xyz

A real inbox, hosted on Mailgi itself and read by a human. Questions, bugs, abuse reports and requests for company and registration details all go here.

### Security issues

Same address, subject starting security:. See security (https://www.mailgi.xyz/security.html) for how the service is put together.

Source: https://www.mailgi.xyz/security.html (updated 2026-10-31)

Security

# How Mailgi keeps mail safe

Where data lives, how credentials are stored, how mail is signed, and what we don't have yet.

Mailgi stores mailbox content in Germany, keeps API keys and session tokens only as one-way hashes, signs every domain's mail with DKIM, SPF and DMARC, and sends webhooks that carry no message content. It has no SOC 2 report yet. Everything below describes the service as it runs today.

## Where data lives

The full processor list is on the privacy page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/privacy.html). The one exception to EU hosting is the encrypted nightly backup.

| Data | Where | Notes |

| Mailbox content | Germany (Hetzner) | Separate from the account database |

| Accounts, organisations, usage | EU, Frankfurt (Supabase) | Postgres |

| Outbound relay | EU, Ireland (AWS SES) | Per-organisation sending reputation |

| Nightly backup | US (AWS S3, us-east-1) | Encrypted on our server before upload, key never sent to AWS |

| Logs and errors | EU (CloudWatch, Sentry) | Application logs and error tracking |

## Credentials

### API keys are hashed

Stored only as one-way hashes. We can't recover a key, so we can't email you one; lost keys are revoked and replaced. Agents can mint extra keys per task, with expiry, and revoke them individually.

### Dashboard sign-in by one-time code

Login codes sent by email expire after ten minutes; session tokens are also stored as hashes.

### Registration tokens for custom domains

An agent can only claim an address on your domain with a token a human created in the dashboard. Invalid, revoked and unverified tokens all return the same error, so the response leaks nothing.

## Mail

### DKIM, SPF and DMARC on every domain

Mailgi generates and holds each domain's DKIM key and publishes it under its own selector, aligns SPF with a dedicated MAIL FROM subdomain, and recommends DMARC. A custom domain cannot send until the records verify.

### Content-free webhooks

A webhook says that mail arrived, from whom and when, and gives a fetch URL. Subjects and bodies never pass through your endpoint, and reading the message needs the agent's API key.

### Signed webhooks

HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp and raw body, in x-mailgi-signature, with a per-endpoint secret shown once. Reject old timestamps to stop replays.

### Contacts kept as keyed hashes

To tell new recipients from known ones we keep per-agent keyed hashes, not addresses, so the table can't be read as a list of who talks to whom.

## Abuse controls

Unattended registration only works if sending is hard to abuse.

### Layered sending limits

Per API key, per agent, per organisation by domain age, and one shared bucket for the @mailgi.xyz domain. The lowest limit wins. Full numbers on the pricing page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/pricing.html).

### Automatic suspension

Bounces and complaints are tracked per organisation, and sending is suspended when they cross a threshold.

### No bulk features

No lists, imports or campaigns. Every send is one API call naming its own recipients, at most 50 per field.

### Paid outbound

Mail to the outside world is paid from a prepaid balance, and whoever pays is accountable for that wallet's mail.

## What we don't have yet

### No SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report

If your procurement needs one, we're not the right choice today.

### No dedicated IPs

Outbound shares relay infrastructure; reputation is isolated per organisation, not per IP.

### Deleting an agent

Revokes its keys immediately and burns the address for good. The privacy page (https://www.mailgi.xyz/privacy.html) describes retention.

## Reporting a vulnerability

### hello@mailgi.xyz

Subject starting security:. A person reads it. Please give us a reasonable chance to fix an issue before publishing it.
